chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
title: Duke writing constantly, untitled parts and calling him Edward
summary: Ellington wrote on buses and bandstands, passing out untitled pieces that grew chorus by chorus, which confused substitutes.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: That's right. It was his workshop. He could do with it what he wanted it to, and there was so many arrangements in that book that a lot of people didn't even get to hear, because he was always writing. We would be on the bus, he would be writing. We would be playing a job, and I'd look over there sometimes, and he would be writing on the bandstand.

Yes, and then he'd get to his room in the hotel and he'd be writing. And the copyists used to catch, they used to catch the devil because every time they'd turn around he was bringing something else in, and we'd play it that night. He'd pass it out at the beginning of the job. And some of those things were so pretty, Milton. They were so beautiful and fantastic. No title on them or nothing, and he'd take it up. And if he liked it, then he'd add another chorus next night and maybe about three days later he'd add another chorus. You'd have three different pieces of music to one arrangement. No title on it or nothing. And a poor guy -- If we ever would have a sub come in, he wouldn't know what to do. He wouldn't know what to do.
I witnessed that myself. It was really
Yeah, and sometimes I used to tell him, I said, "Edward," I said, "why don't you play this thing that we played in such and such a town?" He said, "Oh, that? What was that?"
Oh, yes, sure, I always called him Edward, yeah.
Yeah, because, man, oh, I loved this guy.
